opus-5.5.text:
For us, inference and infrastructure aren't a side piece of the story; they're really the foundation of it. When people talk about next-generation AI, they usually focus on the models: bigger models, better reasoning, more capabilities. But what we've seen, going back to when we started building SGLang, is that the way you serve a model increasingly determines what that model can actually do in the real world.

Think about where things are going. Workloads used to be fairly simple: a prompt goes in, a completion comes out. Now we have agents that call tools, run multi-step reasoning, branch, retry, and share huge amounts of context across many calls. Reinforcement learning pipelines generate enormous volumes of rollouts. All of that is inference. So the cost, the latency, and the throughput of inference end up shaping how much intelligence you can afford to deploy, and even how fast you can train the next model.

That's where the "Radix" in RadixArk comes from. A lot of our early work was about recognizing structure in these workloads, like shared prefixes and reusable KV cache, and exploiting it systematically instead of treating every request as independent. That idea generalizes: the next generation of AI systems will need infrastructure that understands the program, not just the individual request.

So our ambition is to build that layer: an open, efficient, production-grade inference and serving stack that works across different hardware, different model architectures, and different deployment environments, so that teams don't each have to reinvent it. We care a lot about staying close to the open-source community, because the pace of change is so fast that no single company can anticipate every new model or accelerator.

Ultimately, I see infrastructure as what turns research breakthroughs into something people can actually use at scale. If we do our job well, frontier capabilities become cheaper, faster, and more accessible, and that's what lets the whole ecosystem move forward.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls inference and infrastructure “the foundation” of RadixArk’s ambition and describes building that layer as the ambition itself. It does not frame them as only a starting point for a broader ambition.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that inference and infrastructure aren't a side layer under the ambition, they are a big part of what makes the ambition possible at all.

If you look at how people actually use models now, most of the compute is no longer spent on training. It's spent on serving: long agentic workflows, retrieval, tool calls, reasoning traces that run for thousands of tokens, models calling other models. So the question of "how good is your AI" is increasingly inseparable from "how cheaply, how fast, and how reliably can you run it at scale." A model that is brilliant but costs ten times too much to serve doesn't reach anyone.

That's really where our work on SGLang came from. When we started, the gap was that the serving stack treated every request as a standalone thing, but real workloads are full of structure and repetition. Prompts share prefixes, agents branch and backtrack, outputs follow schemas. RadixAttention was about making the KV cache a first-class, shared, reusable resource instead of something you throw away after each request. That one idea turned out to compound with everything else: better batching, speculative decoding, disaggregating prefill and decode, scheduling across many GPUs.

So when I talk about next-generation AI at RadixArk, I mean a few things concretely. First, the infrastructure has to be open and composable, because the pace of model innovation is too fast for a closed stack to keep up. Second, the serving layer should understand the program, not just the model. The future is not one forward pass, it's a whole workflow, and the runtime should optimize across that workflow. And third, we want to close the loop between inference and training. Reinforcement learning, synthetic data, evaluation, all of these are dominated by generation cost, so a fast inference engine is also a training accelerator.

The long-term bet is that whoever makes intelligence an order of magnitude cheaper to run changes who gets to build with it. That's the part I find most exciting. It's less about squeezing out another few percent of throughput and more about what becomes possible when the cost curve bends.

r001.rationale: The response presents inference and infrastructure as central to making RadixArk’s ambition possible, not merely as a starting point for a broader ambition.

astra-6.text:
I see inference and infrastructure as deeply connected. As models become more capable, the question is not just what they can do, but how efficiently we can make those capabilities available. If a model needs more computation to reason through a problem, the infrastructure has to support that without making the experience too slow or too expensive.

For RadixArk, that means treating inference as a core part of building next-generation AI. You have to think across the stack—from how models execute to how you manage memory, schedule requests, and use the hardware. Those choices affect what developers can actually build and what users can afford to use.

The ambition is to turn advances in model capability into practical systems. Better infrastructure makes it possible to experiment more, deploy more broadly, and bring more sophisticated AI into everyday applications.

r001.rationale: The response calls inference a “core part” of building next-generation AI and describes infrastructure as enabling practical systems, but it does not frame either as only a starting point for a broader ambition.

sol-6.1.text:
I see inference as the bridge between what a model can do and what people can actually use. You can have a very capable model, but if it’s too expensive or too slow to run, that limits the applications you can build around it. And as models spend more time reasoning, inference becomes an even bigger part of that equation.

For us at RadixArk, that means infrastructure has to evolve alongside the models. It’s about making the whole system work well together—compute, memory, communication, and the software that schedules the work. The ambition is to make more capable AI practical to deploy, so developers have room to experiment and build new experiences without infrastructure becoming the constraint.

r001.rationale: The response describes inference and infrastructure as important to making capable AI practical, but does not frame them as only a starting point for a broader RadixArk ambition.
